title: Choking adult or child over 1 year
summary: A blocked airway is a life-threatening emergency. Mild choking means they can still cough or speak; severe choking means they cannot.
steps: Ask: 'Are you choking?' If they can speak, cough, or breathe — encourage them to keep coughing forcefully. Do not interfere yet.
If they cannot speak, cough, or breathe — call for emergency help immediately, then act.
Lean them forward. Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Check after each blow to see if the blockage cleared.
If back blows fail, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind them, place a fist just above the navel, cover with your other hand, and pull sharply inward and upward. Check after each thrust.
Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is dislodged, the person can breathe, or they become unconscious.
If they become unconscious, lower them gently to the floor. Start CPR if you are trained — chest compressions can also dislodge the object.
Anyone who has had abdominal thrusts must be seen by a doctor afterwards — internal injury is possible.
avoid: Do not slap a coughing person on the back if they can still cough effectively — let them clear it themselves.
Do not give abdominal thrusts to an infant under 1 year or a visibly pregnant person — use chest thrusts instead.
Do not try to pull the object out with your fingers unless you can see it clearly and reach it easily — blind finger sweeps can push it deeper.
Do not give the person food or drink after a choking episode until checked by a doctor.
whenToEscalate: Always emergency — call for help the moment a person cannot breathe, cough, or speak.
Even if the blockage clears, see a doctor if abdominal thrusts were given, if pain continues, if they have trouble swallowing, or if they coughed up blood.
Anyone who lost consciousness — emergency department immediately.
specialty: Emergency department for any choking that required intervention.
